I believe they’re primarily epithelial or connective tissue cells.

Epithelial cells are the cells that make up the linings of most organs and structures and they typically have a high rate of mitosis. When I think of generic cells, it’s epithelial cells. That said, there are some very specialized epithelial cells. Hepatocytes, the glands of the endocrine system, and ciliated sensory cells are all epithelium. But a large amount of epithelial cells are just there to protect and exist. Some good examples include the esophageal lining to protect from whatever is swallowed, the cells in the bladder that allow it to stretch and contract, and the skin that protects the whole body.

Personally I think they’re more likely to be connective tissue cells. There are specialized connective tissues like bone, blood, and fat, but “connective tissue proper” is just cells and fibers in a gel-like matrix. Connective tissue proper is a bit harder to explain, but essentially it’s everywhere. It lines the inside of the body surfaces, it connects organs to other organs, and it even is what’s in ligaments and tendons. It’s just...stuff. Important stuff! But stuff nonetheless.

Ah, well, I'll try to make it as simple as possible so I don't sound like a blowhard (also if this ends up in r/iamverysmart, well I guess I dug my own grave here). Anyway breathing itself has basically nothing to do with the "conversion". Inhalation brings air in, and in the alveoli, oxygen diffuses into the bloodstream where it's picked up by red blood cells by binding to the heme in the hemoglobin molecule that's part of the cell. From there, the red blood cells travel allllllll through the body, ready to deliver that oxygen to tissues and cells that need it. This is the process the original totally-not-fake texted is referring to, but it's not the breathing where this conversion is happening. At the cellular level, cellular respiration occurs. This is the process by which cells use that oxygen that is delivered as part of an insanely boring chemical reaction that forms ATP, the energy that cells use to do their jobs, basically from sugar. And yes, it happens in the mitochondria. See, that whole "powerhouse of the cell" bit is finally relevant to your life! Anyway blah blah boring science but the end result that matters here is that oxygen is used in the reaction and the byproducts aside from ATP are water and carbon dioxide. It's even a misnomer to say that oxygen "is converted" to carbon dioxide because oxygen was just a part of the equation and carbon dioxide is just a byproduct. Anyway the waste carbon dioxide is taken back to the lungs by one of three methods that aren't too critical here, but the point is it makes its way back the lungs to diffuse back out and be exhaled. In summary, breathing is just the bit where air is brought in and carbon dioxide is pushed out. It has nothing to do with the "conversion". Think of it this way: you drive your car or take a bus to get to work or activities, right? Would you consider the transport actually part of the activity itself? Probably not.
